II.D.3: Explain the core ISO AI standards: 22989, 42001, 42005

html:
1What You Will Learn

  • Explain the OECD principles, the policy recommendations and the recommended practices
  • Explain the NIST AI RMF: functions, categories, subcategories, and the Playbook
  • Explain the three core ISO standards: 22989, 42001 and 42005
  • Tell law, standard and framework apart, and say how they fit together

2II.D.1: Explain the OECD principles and recommended practices

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

Running case

One Stack for Helios

  • Samira Haddad's committee must choose how to organize the program
  • It picks ISO/IEC 42001 to structure the program, the NIST AI RMF to run risk on each system, and the EU AI Act as the legal floor
  • It bases its policy on the OECD principles
  • You must explain what each instrument is for, and why they do not compete

The OECD AI Principles: Origin and Role [Dates]

  • The OECD is an intergovernmental organization; its Recommendation on AI is a non-binding standard that many governments follow
  • It was first adopted in 2019 and updated in May 2024
  • It sets five values-based principles for AI actors and five recommendations for policy-makers
  • Its definition of an AI system (module 1) was reused in other laws and frameworks
  • It is soft law: it shapes policy and legislation but is not itself enforced
Exam tip

The OECD principles are values for governments and organizations; they are not a certification or a statute.

The Five Values-Based Principles

  • 1.1 Inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being: responsible stewardship of trustworthy AI for people and the planet
  • 1.2 Human rights and democratic values, including fairness and privacy: respect the rule of law, with safeguards such as human oversight
  • 1.3 Transparency and explainability: responsible disclosure and meaningful information about systems
  • 1.4 Robustness, security and safety: across the whole lifecycle, with the ability to override, repair or decommission safely
  • 1.5 Accountability: for proper functioning, with traceability and a systematic risk management approach to each lifecycle phase

Exam tip

Safe decommissioning and systematic risk management are the OECD's practical hooks for organizations.

Recommendations for Policy-Makers

  • 2.1 investing in AI research and development
  • 2.2 fostering an inclusive AI-enabling ecosystem
  • 2.3 shaping an enabling, interoperable governance and policy environment
  • 2.4 building human capacity and preparing for labor-market transformation
  • 2.5 international co-operation for trustworthy AI
  • These are aimed at governments; organizations meet them through policy engagement and skills programs

Exam tip

Principles are for AI actors; recommendations are for governments.

The OECD Framework and Recommended Practices

  • Classification framework: the OECD classifies AI systems along five dimensions: people and planet, economic context, data and input, AI model, and task and output (NIST adapted it for its own lifecycle figure)
  • Lifecycle thinking: apply risk management to each phase, from design to retirement
  • Recommended practices for actors: traceability of data, processes and decisions; responsible business conduct with suppliers; cooperation across the AI value chain
  • Safety valve: systems that cause undue harm can be overridden, repaired or decommissioned
  • Tools: the OECD.AI observatory collects policies and tools for trustworthy AI
Exam tip

The OECD framework helps you describe a system (its context, data, model, task); it is not a compliance checklist.

3II.D.2: Explain the NIST AI RMF and its Playbook

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 2 practice questions on this indicator.

The NIST AI RMF at a Glance [Dates] [Verify live]

  • NIST AI RMF 1.0 was released in January 2023; it is voluntary, sector-agnostic and meant to be a living document
  • A formal review is expected no later than 2028
  • Part 1: foundations: framing AI risk, the audience, trustworthy characteristics, effectiveness
  • Part 2: the Core: 4 functions, 19 categories, 72 subcategories; then profiles
  • The Playbook (online) suggests actions; the generative AI profile applies it to generative AI
  • As of 27 October 2026: NIST's Playbook page says the framework is being updated; check the current version

Exam tip

The AI RMF is guidance, not law and not a certification: organizations choose how much of it to use.

The Seven Trustworthy Characteristics

  • Valid and reliable (the foundation), safe, secure and resilient
  • Accountable and transparent (runs through all)
  • Explainable and interpretable
  • Privacy-enhanced
  • Fair, with harmful bias managed
  • Tradeoffs are usual: balance them by context, and justify the choice openly (module 1)
  • Trustworthiness is only as strong as its weakest characteristic

Exam tip

Seven characteristics, one foundation: if the system is not valid and reliable, nothing above it helps.

The Core: Four Functions

  • GOVERN: a cross-cutting culture, policies, accountability and structures
  • MAP: frame the context and risks of a specific system
  • MEASURE: analyze, assess and track risks with metrics and tests
  • MANAGE: prioritize and treat risks, with response and recovery
  • The actions are not a checklist and need no fixed order; after GOVERN is in place, most users start with MAP, then MEASURE and MANAGE, and iterate

Exam tip

GOVERN applies to everything; the other three apply system by system.

GOVERN: Culture, Accountability and Policy

Category What it covers
GOVERN 1 policies, processes and practices; legal requirements; risk tolerance; inventory; decommissioning
GOVERN 2 accountability structures; roles; training; executive responsibility
GOVERN 3 diversity, equity, inclusion and accessibility in risk work
GOVERN 4 a culture that considers and communicates AI risk
GOVERN 5 engagement with relevant AI actors
GOVERN 6 third-party software, data and supply-chain risks
  • 6 categories, 19 subcategories; modules 2 and 3 used several (for example GOVERN 2.1 on roles and GOVERN 6.1 on third parties)
Exam tip

GOVERN is about the organization's rules and culture; it is not tied to one system.

MAP: Context and Impacts

Category What it covers
MAP 1 context is established and understood (intended purposes, laws, settings)
MAP 2 the AI system is categorized (its tasks and methods)
MAP 3 capabilities, usage, goals, benefits and costs against benchmarks
MAP 4 risks and benefits of all components, including third-party
MAP 5 impacts on individuals, groups, communities, organizations and society
  • 5 categories, 18 subcategories
  • MAP ends with enough context to inform an initial go or no-go decision
  • MAP 1.1: intended purposes, beneficial uses, laws and norms, and settings are understood and documented
Exam tip

If a question is about who is affected and what the system is for, the function is MAP.

MEASURE: Metrics, Testing and Tracking

Category What it covers
MEASURE 1 appropriate methods and metrics are identified and applied
MEASURE 2 the system is evaluated for trustworthy characteristics
MEASURE 3 mechanisms track identified risks over time
MEASURE 4 feedback about the efficacy of measurement is gathered
  • 4 categories, 22 subcategories
  • Uses quantitative, qualitative or mixed methods; systems are tested before deployment and regularly in operation (TEVV: test, evaluation, verification and validation)
  • MEASURE 2.11: fairness and bias are evaluated and documented
  • Independent review can improve the testing and reduce internal bias
Exam tip

Measuring is how you know whether a risk is real; MANAGE is what you do about it.

MANAGE: Prioritize, Respond and Recover

Category What it covers
MANAGE 1 risks are prioritized, responded to and managed
MANAGE 2 strategies to maximize benefits and minimize impacts
MANAGE 3 third-party risks and benefits are managed
MANAGE 4 risk treatments, response, recovery and communication plans
  • 4 categories, 13 subcategories
  • MANAGE 1.2: treatment is prioritized by impact, likelihood and available resources
  • MANAGE 2.4: mechanisms to supersede, disengage or deactivate systems that behave outside intended use
  • MANAGE 4.1: post-deployment monitoring plans, with appeal and override, decommissioning, incident response and change management
Exam tip

Deactivation, incident response and monitoring plans are MANAGE items.

The Playbook, Profiles and the Generative AI Profile Beyond the BoK [Dates] [Verify live]

  • Playbook: suggested actions for each subcategory; voluntary, not a checklist; a living resource updated about twice a year, in several formats
  • Use-case profiles: the Core applied to a setting, such as a hiring profile
  • Temporal profiles: a current and a target profile; the gap between them becomes the action plan
  • Cross-sectoral profiles: topics such as large language models, cloud services or acquisition
  • Generative AI profile (July 2024): defines twelve generative-AI risks and maps actions to the four functions
  • As of 27 October 2026: the Playbook will follow the framework's update

Exam tip

Current profile, target profile, gap, action plan: that is how profiles drive improvement.

4II.D.3: Explain the core ISO AI standards: 22989, 42001, 42005

Exam angle

The BoK verb is Understand, so the depth is Understand. The course has 1 practice question on this indicator.

ISO/IEC 22989: A Shared Language

  • ISO/IEC 22989 sets out AI concepts and terminology: what words such as AI system, machine learning, bias and robustness mean
  • It describes stakeholder roles across the AI value chain and lifecycle concepts
  • Its AI system definition (an engineered system generating outputs for human-defined objectives, module 1) feeds NIST and other documents
  • It is a vocabulary standard: it gives no requirements and cannot be certified against
  • Depth marker: taught from the BoK and public summaries; the standard is paid and was not read
Exam tip

22989 is the dictionary; 42001 is the certifiable management system.

ISO/IEC 42001: The AI Management System [Dates]

  • ISO/IEC 42001 (published December 2023) sets requirements for an AI management system (AIMS): an organization-wide system to govern AI responsibly
  • Same harmonized structure as ISO 27001 and ISO 9001: clauses 4 to 10 in a plan-do-check-act cycle
  • 4 context, 5 leadership and AI policy, 6 planning (risk and impact assessment), 7 support, 8 operation (lifecycle processes), 9 performance evaluation (audit, review), 10 improvement
  • It is certifiable by accredited bodies
  • Depth marker: taught from public summaries; the standard is paid and was not read

Exam tip

A management system is a continuing process of policy, risk, operation, audit and improvement, not a one-time project.

ISO/IEC 42001: Controls and Certification

  • Annex A: a reference set of 38 controls in nine control objectives (for example AI policy, internal organization, resources, impact assessment, life cycle, data, information for parties, use, third-party relationships)
  • Selection is risk-based: the organization chooses controls and records its choices in a statement of applicability
  • Annex B: implementation guidance; Annex C: AI-related risk sources; Annex D: use across sectors
  • Certification: an accredited body audits the AIMS; a certificate shows the system meets the standard, not that a product is safe or legal
  • Helios: uses 42001 to give the program a structure that auditors recognize
Exam tip

A 42001 certificate covers the organization's management system; it is not proof that a given AI system complies with a law.

ISO/IEC 42005: AI System Impact Assessment [Dates]

  • ISO/IEC 42005 (published 27 May 2025) gives guidance, not requirements, for AI system impact assessment
  • It covers how and when to assess how a system and its foreseeable uses may affect individuals and society, and at which life-cycle stages
  • It covers documentation, including approval and review
  • It is for organizations of any size, and the assessment can be integrated with AI risk management and the management system
  • Link: 42001 asks for AI system impact assessment; 42005 explains how to do it
  • Depth marker: taught from public summaries

Exam tip

42001 requires impact assessment inside the management system; 42005 is the guidance on how to perform it.

Law, Standard, Framework: How They Fit

  • EU AI Act: binding law; sets duties and penalties; Helios's legal floor
  • OECD principles: soft law; values that shape policy; Helios's policy basis
  • NIST AI RMF: voluntary framework; a risk process run system by system
  • ISO/IEC 42001: certifiable standard; the management structure of the program
  • ISO/IEC 22989 and 42005: vocabulary and impact-assessment guidance
  • ISO/IEC 23894 (one row only): guidance on AI risk management
  • They work together; only law is mandatory, and standards can help show compliance

Exam tip

Question stems often ask what an instrument is: binding law, soft law, voluntary framework or certifiable standard.

5Exam Q&A

5.1 Practice questions (one best answer, or select exactly the number the question asks for)

S1Which list correctly names the OECD's five values-based principles for trustworthy AI?

  • AInclusive growth, profitability and competitiveness, transparency, robustness, accountability for outcomes
  • BHuman oversight, fairness, privacy, transparency, and innovation and market access for firms
  • CInclusive growth, human rights and fairness, innovation incentives, security, accountability of regulators
  • DInclusive growth, human rights and fairness, transparency, robustness and safety, accountability
Show the answer

Answer: D. The five principles are inclusive growth, sustainable development and well-being; human rights and democratic values, including fairness and privacy; transparency and explainability; robustness, security and safety; and accountability. Option D gives them in short form, and the other lists swap in items that are not OECD principles.

S2Helios's committee wants to document the intended purpose, the legal context, the affected groups and the expected benefits of the new assistant before it is tested. Which NIST AI RMF function does this work belong to?

  • AMANAGE, because the work prioritizes and treats risks identified for the assistant
  • BGOVERN, because policies and accountability must be set before a system is described
  • CMAP, because it establishes the context and impacts of a specific system
  • DMEASURE, because it evaluates the assistant against metrics and test results
Show the answer

Answer: C. MAP establishes context: intended purposes, legal context, settings, benefits and the impacts on people. MEASURE comes after, MANAGE treats the mapped and measured risks, and GOVERN sets the organization-wide policies rather than describing one system.

S3Which TWO statements about the NIST AI RMF Playbook are correct? (Select TWO.)

  • AUsing the Playbook is mandatory for organizations that sell AI products in the United States
  • BIts suggestions are voluntary, and it is not a checklist to be followed in its entirety
  • CCompleting the Playbook earns an organization a certificate recognized by accreditation bodies
  • DIt replaces the Core and the need to choose among the categories and subcategories
  • EIt suggests actions that organizations can adapt for each subcategory of the Core
Show the answer

Answer: B, E. The Playbook offers voluntary suggested actions aligned to the Core's subcategories, and organizations tailor them. It is not mandatory, not a certification scheme and not a replacement for the Core.

S4How does ISO/IEC 42001 differ from the NIST AI RMF?

  • AISO/IEC 42001 is a binding law that regulators enforce, while the NIST AI RMF is only a glossary
  • BThe NIST AI RMF is a certifiable standard, while ISO/IEC 42001 is a voluntary risk-assessment checklist
  • CBoth documents are voluntary guidance with no requirements, so an organization is not audited against either
  • DISO/IEC 42001 sets requirements for an AI management system that an organization can be certified against
Show the answer

Answer: D. ISO/IEC 42001 specifies requirements for an AI management system and is certifiable by accredited bodies. The NIST AI RMF is voluntary guidance with no certification. Neither is a binding law.

6Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
OECD five principles (inclusive growth; human rights, fairness and privacy; transparency and explainability; robustness, security and safety; accountability) and five policy recommendations
NIST AI RMF voluntary; four functions, 19 categories, 72 subcategories; GOVERN cross-cuts, MAP then MEASURE then MANAGE; Playbook and profiles
ISO 22989 vocabulary; 42001 certifiable management system; 42005 impact-assessment guidance
Fit law is binding; the others are soft law, framework, standard and guidance
